paragraph: Angola's [Presidential Decree 202/11](<https://lex.ao/docs/presidente-da-republica/2011/decreto-presidencial-n-o-202-11-de-22-de-julho/>), published on 22 July 2011, approves the regulation on information society technologies and services. It covers electronic documents, qualified electronic signatures, certification and electronic contracts. In the last twelve months, on 30 July 2026 the Assembleia Nacional [approved, by 166 votes,](<https://www.opais.ao/politica/parlamento-aprova-autorizacao-legislativa-sobre-assinatura-electronica-com-166-votos-a-favor/>) a bill authorising the President to legislate a regime for electronic signatures and digital certification. That regime has not been enacted. No decree, regulation or order made under the 2011 decree has been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Burundi's [Loi N°1/22 of 22 August 2024](<https://arct.gov.bi/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/LOI_COMMUNICATIONS-ELECTRONIQUES.pdf>) is the code des communications électroniques et postales. In the last twelve months, on 29 May 2026 the regulator ARCT published [national e-commerce ecosystem guidelines](<https://arct.gov.bi/2026/05/29/lignes-directrices-de-lecosysteme-national-de-commerce-electronique-du-burundi/>) on interoperability, transaction security and consumer protection. On 26 June 2026 it [called e-commerce platforms and merchant sites to declare their conformity](<https://web.archive.org/web/20260729212203/https://arct.gov.bi/2026/06/26/appel-a-la-declaratio-n-de-conformite-des-plateformes-et-sites-marchands-de-commerce-electronique-au-burundi/>) under the code. It annexed a procedures manual, a conformity checklist and a declaration form. No declaration of conformity received, licence or penalty under the code has been found.

Benin's [Loi n° 2017-20, the Code du numérique](<https://sgg.gouv.bj/doc/loi-2017-20/download>), was promulgated on 20 April 2018. It includes a title on the obligations of trust service providers. In the last twelve months, [Decree 2025-363 of 2 July 2025](<https://sgg.gouv.bj/doc/decret-2025-363/>) set the conditions for providers of electronic archiving, who must be qualified by the competent authority as trust service providers for three years at a time. No accreditation, licence or penalty under the code in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

Burkina Faso's [Law n°045-2009/AN](<https://www.ictpolicyafrica.org/api/documents/download?_id=5eb968597c7814001bc4bcbe>), promulgated on 4 December 2009, regulates electronic services and transactions. It covers electronic signatures, e-commerce contracts and trust service providers. In the last twelve months, [a report on the launch of FasoSign](<https://cfinance.news/article/burkina-fasomodernisation-de-ladministration-publique-le-premier-ministre-lance-la-plateforme-fasosign-pour-boucler-la-boucle-de-la-dematerialisation/>) on 15 September 2026 said the platform gives effect to the law and its implementing decrees. The decrees are not named. No accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

Botswana's [Electronic Communications and Transactions Act, 2014 (Act No. 14)](<https://www.bocra.org.bw/sites/default/files/documents/Electronic-Communications-and-Transactions-Act-2014.pdf>) was assented to on 14 May 2014. It gives electronic communications, contracts and signatures legal effect and covers the protection of consumers who buy online. The regulator BOCRA records the Act as in force since 1 April 2016. No change has been found in the last twelve months. The only instrument found that was made under the Act is the [ministerial Order that brought it into force](<https://www.bocra.org.bw/sites/default/files/documents/Electronic-Communications-and-Transactions-Act-2014.pdf>). Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

The regulator ARCEP lists [Loi 22.002 of 11 January 2022, regulating electronic transactions in the country](<https://www.arcep.cf/fr/index.php/reglementation/lois-et-ordonnances>), on its official index of laws and ordinances. The index page was published on 21 February 2024 and presents the law as one of the country's laws. No change has been found in the last twelve months. The index shows no decree, regulation or order made under the law, and the text of the law has not been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Côte d'Ivoire's [Loi n°2013-546 of 30 July 2013 on electronic transactions](<https://anssi.gouv.ci/documents/41/Decret_2014-106_12_mars_2014.pdf>) is the law that a decree of 12 March 2014 states it implements. That decree sets rules on secure electronic signatures and qualified electronic certificates, and on the approval of certification service providers by ARTCI. [Ordinance 2024-950 of 30 October 2024 repealed its Article 50](<https://www.anssi.ci/documents/21/Ordonnace_N2024-950_du_30_octobre_portant_modification_de_lordonnance_sur_les_e-services_et_abrogation.pdf>) and left the rest in place. In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed: [AIP reported on 25 July 2026](<https://www.aip.ci/cote-divoire-aip-lanssi-met-en-service-linfrastructure-a-cles-publiques-nationale/>) that the national public key infrastructure was in service. No accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

Cameroon's [Law No. 2010/021 of 21 December 2010](<https://www.mincommerce.gov.cm/sites/default/files/documents/loi-n-2010-021-du-21-decembre-2010-regissant-le-commerce-electronique-au-cameroun.pdf>) governs electronic commerce. It defines electronic signatures, certificates and certification authorities. [Decree no. 2011/1521/PM of 15 June 2011](<https://www.mincommerce.gov.cm/sites/default/files/documents/decret-n-2011-1521-pm-du-15-juin-2011-fixant-les-modalites-d-application-de-la-loi-regissant-le-commerce-electronique-au-cameroun.pdf>), issued by the Prime Minister, fixes the modalities of its application. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

DR Congo's [Ordonnance-loi n° 23/010 of 13 March 2023, the Code du Numérique](<https://are.gouv.cd/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/04042023-ORDONNANCE-LOI-23-010-DU-13-MARS-PORTANT-CODE-DU-NUMERIQUE_compressed.pdf>), governs electronic writings, electronic signatures, trust service providers and digital services. In the last twelve months, [the ministerial order of 11 March 2026](<https://www.scribd.com/document/1015223474/Arre-te-Ministeriel-N-Cab-MIN-ECONUM-AKIM-MLNS-ALM-004-2026-du-11-mars-2026>) set an authorisation regime for qualified trust-service providers, marketplaces and e-commerce platforms. [ACP reports it was published on 17 March 2026](<https://acp.cd/economie/activites-numeriques-en-rdc-publication-officielle-de-larrete-fixant-les-conditions-dautorisation/>), with a transition to 30 June 2026. No authorisation granted under it, and no other accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years, has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

The Congo's [Loi n° 37-2019 of 12 December 2019 on electronic transactions](<https://sgg.cg/JO/2026/congo-jo-2026-29-4.pdf>) is cited as a legal basis by four arrêtés of 9 July 2026. [Décret n° 2026-101 of 31 March 2026](<https://sgg.cg/JO/2026/congo-jo-2026-28.pdf>) cites the same law. Both concern the certified electronic invoicing system, and both treat the law as existing. In the last twelve months the law was cited and not changed. No decree, regulation or order made under it is named in the sources found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

The UNECA Digital Trade Regulatory Integration profile, published in 2024, states that the Comoros's 2021 law on cyber security and the fight against cybercrime, Law No. 21-012/AU, [fills gaps in electronic transactions](<https://dtri.uneca.org/v1/uploads/country-profile/com-country-profile-en.pdf>). It gives electronic signatures the same legal effect as handwritten ones. The profile also states that the Comoros has no stand-alone law on electronic transactions. No change has been found in the last twelve months. The profile [names no decree, regulation or order made under it and no provider accredited under it](<https://dtri.uneca.org/v1/uploads/country-profile/com-country-profile-en.pdf>). Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

In July 2025 [the Secretary of State for the Digital Economy, Pedro Lopes, cited Cape Verde's modern laws on data protection and digital transactions](<https://www.wearetech.africa/en/fils-uk/news/public-management/cape-verde-ramps-up-digital-start-up-ecosystem-to-boost-economy>) as regulatory progress. The report was published on 31 July 2025 and is the only statement found on the law on digital transactions. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No decree, regulation or order made under the law is named in the sources found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Djibouti's National Assembly [adopted the Digital Code unanimously on 30 June 2025](<https://www.lanation.dj/le-code-du-numerique-un-pas-decisif-pour-la-transformation-digitale/>). The text has nearly 800 articles and covers the regulation of online commerce among other areas. [Jones Day reports](<https://www.jonesday.com/en/insights/2025/07/national-assembly-of-the-republic-of-djibouti-approves-digital-code>) that the law was still to be promulgated by the President and published in the Journal Officiel, and that it is to be supplemented by regulatory decrees. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Whether the Digital Code has been promulgated or is in force has not been found. Establishing would need a law in force on electronic contracts, signatures or online sales.

Algeria's [Law No. 18-05 of 10 May 2018](<https://www.mpt.gov.dz/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Loi-n%C2%B0-18-05-du-10-mai-2018.-fr_0_0.pdf>) sets general rules for e-commerce. It covers registration of e-suppliers, electronic contracts, payment, advertising and penalties. [UNCTAD's Global Cyberlaw Tracker lists Executive Decree 19-89 of 5 March 2019](<https://unctad.org/topic/ecommerce-and-digital-economy/ecommerce-law-reform/summary-adoption-e-commerce-legislation-worldwide>) as Algeria's electronic transactions legislation, and it fixes how registers of electronic commercial transactions are kept. In the last twelve months, [Law 26-02 of 17 February 2026](<https://www.tsa-algerie.com/lalgerie-lance-un-portail-electronique-dedie-au-marches-publics/>) set rules on trust services for electronic transactions. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under Law 18-05 has been found in the last three years. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

Egypt's [Law No. 15/2004 regulating e-signatures was issued on 21 April 2004](<https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/legislation/details/13546>). It gives electronic signatures and electronic writing the evidential effect of paper, and sets up ITIDA to license certificate issuers. A [law firm's ICLG chapter of July 2025](<https://web.archive.org/web/20251004195804/https://iclg.com/practice-areas/data-protection-laws-and-regulations/egypt>) states that its executive regulations require e-signature applicants to secure the confidentiality of information. In the last twelve months it was cited and not changed. In November 2026 [a Public Prosecution course named the law](<https://www.youm7.com/story/2026/11/11/%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%86%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%A8%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%A9-%D8%AA%D8%B7%D9%84%D9%82-%D8%A8%D8%B1%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%AC%D9%8B%D8%A7-%D9%85%D8%AA%D8%AE%D8%B5%D8%B5%D9%8B%D8%A7-%D9%84%D8%AD%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%8A%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B4%D8%AE%D8%B5%D9%8A%D8%A9/7614234>) among those related to data protection. No accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

No stage is set. No law or draft on electronic transactions or e-commerce is on record for Eritrea as at September 2026. No source dated in the last three years says the country has none. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Absent would need a source from the past three years that says the country has no law on electronic transactions or e-commerce and no draft of one.

Ethiopia's electronic signature law is [Proclamation No. 1072/2017](<https://www.ena.et/web/eng/w/eng_7816242>), with its amendment. In November 2025 the Council of Ministers [unanimously approved the Electronic Signature regulation](<https://www.ena.et/web/eng/w/eng_7816242>) under the proclamation, to take effect on publication in the Federal Negarit Gazette. The Ethiopian News Agency called the regulation a step toward fully operationalizing the law. No change has been found in the last twelve months, and no publication of the regulation has been found. No accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

Gabon's [Law No. 025/2021 of 28 December 2021](<https://journal-officiel.ga/18190-025-2021-/>) regulates electronic transactions. It gives electronic acts, writings, signatures and invoices the same probative force as paper. It also sets rules for e-commerce, distance contracts and consumer withdrawal. In the last twelve months, on 18 September 2026 the [Council of Ministers adopted a draft decree](<https://agpgabon.ga/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Communique-Final-du-18-septembre-2026-version-Presse-ecrite.pdf>) setting how the qualified signature certificate and other trust services are issued. It covers approval conditions and duties of providers. No accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

Ghana's 2008 Electronic Transactions Act is in force, and the [US Country Commercial Guide, published 20 September 2024, calls it the baseline for e-commerce and e-signature](<https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/ghana-digital-economy>). In November 2023 the Ministry of Communications and Digitalisation [issued an enforcement notice under the Act](<https://digitalpolicyalert.org/digest/dpa-digital-digest-ghana>). It required all e-commerce platforms and digital delivery companies to register by January 2024. In the last twelve months the Act was cited and not changed: a [MyJoyOnline op-ed of 16 October 2026 names the Act as part of Ghana's existing legal foundation](<https://www.myjoyonline.com/bold-ambitions-fragile-foundations-is-ghana-ready-for-the-ai-and-data-centre-risks-it-is-inviting/>). No decree, regulation or order made under the Act is named in the sources found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Guinea's [Law L/2016/035/AN of 26 July 2016 on electronic transactions](<https://anssi.gov.gn/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/loi_l-2016-035-an_relative_aux_transactions_electroniques.pdf>) applies to all electronic transactions including online commerce. [Decree D/2021/092/PRG/SGG, signed on 25 March 2021](<https://anssi.gov.gn/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/DECRET-D-2021-092-PRG-SGG-Copie-2.pdf>), names the ARPT as regulator with sanction powers. In the last twelve months, a presidential decree signed on 19 August 2026 [gives an electronic signature the same probative force as a paper writing](<https://www.guinee360.com/19/08/2026/guinee-mamadi-doumbouya-officialise-la-signature-electronique/>) and requires every electronic-certification service provider to be approved by ANDE. On 20 November 2026 the minister said [the decree's regulatory framework and implementing orders were complete](<https://mediaguinee.com/2026/11/confiance-numerique-en-guinee-apres-quatre-jours-de-travaux-une-feuille-de-route-elaboree-pour-loperationnalisation-de-la-signature-electronique/>). No accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

[UNCTAD's Global Cyberlaw Tracker lists the Information and Communications Act No. 2 of 2009](<https://unctad.org/topic/ecommerce-and-digital-economy/ecommerce-law-reform/summary-adoption-e-commerce-legislation-worldwide>) as The Gambia's electronic transactions legislation. A first reading of the Communications Bill 2025 took place on 19 November 2025. In the last twelve months, [the National Assembly approved the Communications Bill 2025 at second reading on 2 March 2026](<https://standard.gm/lawmakers-back-bill-to-protect-personal-data-in-digital-age/>). The Minister said it will recognise electronic signatures and contracts and cover electronic commerce services. No source found reports that it has been enacted. No decree, regulation or order made under the 2009 Act on electronic transactions has been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

In May 2026 Guinea-Bissau's regulator ARN-TIC [put the draft Electronic Transactions Law out for public consultation, with responses due by 28 May 2026](<https://www.odemocratagb.com/?p=57171>). The [112-article text would give data messages, electronic records, contracts and electronic signatures legal effect](<https://arn.gw/site24/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Lei_Transaccoes_Electronicas_Revisada_PT.docx>). In the last twelve months, on 17 November 2026 [the Council of Ministers examined the proposed Electronic Transactions Law](<https://ang.gw/governo-analisa-novas-leis-sobre-economia-digital-e-proteccao-social-no-pais/>), and on 24 November 2026 it [approved the bill with amendments](<https://ang.gw/conselho-de-ministros-aprova-proposta-do-oge-para-2027-no-valor-de-5436-mil-milhoes-de-francos-cfa/>). The text enters into force only on a date the Minister designates. No law in force has been found. Establishing would need a law in force on electronic contracts, signatures or online sales.

The official gazette compilation of Equatorial Guinea, published 10 January 2017, [lists Ley Núm. 2/2.017, of 10 January 2017, on Firma y Documentos Electrónicos](<https://palaciodelpueblo.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/LEYES-ELECTRONICAS.pdf>), as a law of the country. The entry gives its title and date, so what the law requires has not been found. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found, and nothing found shows the law being applied. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Kenya's [Business Laws (Amendment) Act, 2020 came into force on 18 March 2020](<https://www.dlapiperafrica.com/en/kenya/insights/2020/what-it-means-to-use-electronic-signatures.html>). It allows advanced electronic signatures in place of wet-ink signatures in nearly all legal documents. On 1 September 2020 the Communications Authority [required all foreign electronic certification providers to apply for recognition within 30 days](<https://www.dlapiperafrica.com/en/kenya/insights/2020/what-it-means-to-use-electronic-signatures.html>). As at October 2020 [only two certification service providers were licensed](<https://www.dlapiperafrica.com/en/kenya/insights/2020/what-it-means-to-use-electronic-signatures.html>), and neither had started issuing advanced electronic signatures. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law dated in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

Liberia's [Electronic Transactions Law, Chapter 13 of Title 14 of the General Business Law](<https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/acc_e/lbr_e/WTACCLBR15_LEG_18.pdf>), was approved on 8 January 2002 and published on 19 June 2002. It gives electronic records, contracts and signatures legal effect. The law [applies at once to matters under Titles 5 and 21 of the General Business Law](<https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/acc_e/lbr_e/WTACCLBR15_LEG_18.pdf>). Elsewhere it applies only as regulations of the Minister of Foreign Affairs bring it into effect. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No such regulation, and no decree or order made under the law, has been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Libya's [Law No. 6 of 2022 on Electronic Transactions](<https://lawsociety.ly/legislation/%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%88%D9%86-%D8%B1%D9%82%D9%85-6-%D9%84%D8%B3%D9%86%D8%A9-2022-%D9%85-%D8%A8%D8%B4%D8%A3%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B9%D8%A7%D9%85%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A5%D9%84%D9%83/>) was issued by the House of Representatives on 4 October 2022. It gives electronic signatures, records and contracts legal effect, and sets pre-contract disclosure and return rules for online sellers. In December 2023 Eltumi Partners [stated that the government had not yet published the executive regulation](<https://eltumipartners.com/2023/12/data-protection-under-libya-e-transactions-law/>) to the law. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No regulation, order or decision made under the law is named. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

The government opened a [two-day validation workshop in Maseru on 28 September 2026](<https://www.gov.ls/development/micsti-on-electronic-transactions-communications-bill/>) on the Electronic Transactions and Communications Bill, 2026, which revises a 2022 bill of the same name. The ministry responsible says Lesotho [lacks a legal and regulatory framework for electronic transactions](<https://www.itweb.africa/article/lesotho-revises-electronic-transactions-bill/KA3WwMdzPLDvrydZ>). In the last twelve months the bill reached validation, and the draft is to go next to the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel for refinement. No passage date has been found, and no law in force has been found. Establishing would need a law in force on electronic contracts, signatures or online sales.

Morocco's [Law 43-20 on trust services for electronic transactions](<https://www.dgssi.gov.ma/fr/loi-ndeg43-20-relative-aux-services-de-confiance-pour-les-transactions>) was promulgated on 31 December 2020. It covers signatures and certificates, not online selling. [Decree 2-22-687 of 16 November 2022 was made to apply the law](<https://www.dgssi.gov.ma/fr/prestations-et-produits-reglementes/>). [The DGSSI approved Damanesign as a trust service provider on 3 March 2025](<https://www.dgssi.gov.ma/sites/default/files/2025-03/decision_d_agremenent_DAMANESIGN_2025.pdf>). In May 2025 [the Mouvement populaire group filed a private bill](<https://lematin.ma/nation/le-mp-veut-encadrer-le-commerce-electronique/280553>) adding a chapter on online selling to consumer protection Law 31.08. In the last twelve months, in September 2026 the DGSSI named three approved providers: EURAFRIC INFORMATION, Barid Al Maghrib and DamaneSign. It also [lists the conformity certificates it has issued](<https://www.dgssi.gov.ma/fr/prestations-et-produits-reglementes/>), six of them current, the latest dated 18 March 2026.

Madagascar's [transactions law, Loi no. 2014-024](<https://www.africa-laws.org/Madagascar/Comercial%20law/Loi-n%C2%B02014-024-du-10-12-2014_sur-Les-Transactions-Electroniques.pdf>), dated 10 December 2014, defines electronic signature and regulates e-commerce. A separate law of the same date covers electronic signature. Decree 2024-1911, published on 13 November 2024, gives documents signed through a certified electronic signature device the same recognition as paper, and cites both laws as its legal basis. In September 2025 Newsmada reported that a [draft decree on electronic signature and interoperability was in preparation](<https://newsmada.com/2025/09/13/signature-electronique-et-interoperabilite-madagascar-renforce-le-cadre-juridique/>). No change has been found in the last twelve months, and no source found says the draft decree has been adopted. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Mali's [Law no. 2016-012 of 6 May 2016 on electronic transactions, exchanges and services](<https://sgg-mali.ml/JO/2016/mali-jo-2016-22.pdf>) regulates electronic commerce. It gives legal effect to electronic writings, signatures, certificates and archiving, and was published in the Journal officiel of 27 May 2016. In November 2025 the Director General of Taxes cited the [law on electronic transactions as part of a solid legal framework](<https://www.maliweb.net/interview/hamadou-fall-dianka-dg-des-impots-le-montant-des-recettes-electroniques-a-atteint-300-milliards-de-fcfa-en-2024-3111560.html>) for digitalising public payments. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No decree, regulation or order made under the 2016 law is named in the sources found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Mozambique's Electronic Transactions Law, [Law no. 3/2017 of 9 January](<https://www.dlapiperdataprotection.com/guide.pdf?c=MZ>), sets rules on electronic marketing consent, intermediary service providers and personal data, with fines for breach. [Decree no. 59/2023 of 27 October, amended by Decree no. 44/2025 of 28 November, requires intermediary electronic service providers and digital platform operators to register](<https://www.dlapiperdataprotection.com/guide.pdf?c=MZ>) and be licensed with INTIC. In the last twelve months, on 8 June 2026 INTIC's board president [said 19 licences had been issued](<https://techafricanews.com/2026/06/08/mozambique-issues-first-licenses-to-digital-operators-in-major-regulatory-milestone/>). About 170 registered companies were under evaluation. Decree No. 40/2026 [gives the electronic signature the same legal standing as a handwritten one](<https://360mozambique.com/development/government-approves-regulation-allowing-certificates-for-low-risk-activities-to-be-issued-within-two-hours/>). No enforcement figure beyond the licences has been found.

Mauritania's [Law no. 2018-022 of 12 June 2018 on electronic exchanges](<https://techrek.info/fr/approbation-de-la-creation-dune-agence-nationale-de-cybersecurite-et-de-certification-electronique/>) is the law under which Tech Rek reports a draft decree. It reported on 23 April 2024 [a draft decree made under the 2018 law](<https://techrek.info/fr/approbation-de-la-creation-dune-agence-nationale-de-cybersecurite-et-de-certification-electronique/>), headed as approving a national agency for cybersecurity and electronic certification. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No source has been found on whether the draft decree was adopted, and no decree, regulation or order made under the 2018 law has been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Mauritius passed [Act No. 5 of 2026, the Electronic Transactions (Amendment) Act](<https://mauritiusassembly.govmu.org/mauritiusassembly/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Act0526.pdf>), on 19 May 2026 and assented to it on 25 May. Law firm Appleby says it [recognises electronic signatures, electronic transferable records and contracts formed by automated systems](<https://www.applebyglobal.com/publications/from-e-signatures-to-ai-driven-contracts-how-mauritius-is-rewriting-the-rules-of-digital-transactions/>). It comes into operation on a date to be fixed by Proclamation. In the last twelve months, on 29 July 2026 the ICT minister said [the amendments had modernised the framework for digital commerce](<https://mitci.govmu.org/mitci/ict-minister-calls-for-stronger-cybersecurity-for-postal-sector/>). The Electronic Transactions Act 2006 is treated as existing law. No regulation made under either Act has been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Malawi's [Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act, Act 33 of 2016, commenced on 1 June 2017](<https://malawilii.org/akn/mw/act/2016/33/eng@2017-12-31>). It gives legal effect to electronic writing, electronic signatures and digital signature certificates. In February 2024 the government [put draft regulations on cryptography and certification authorities to stakeholders](<https://digmap.pppc.mw/government-engages-stakeholders-on-etca-regulations/>). In the last twelve months, in October 2026 the ICT minister said the government would [review the Act and introduce an E-Transactions and E-Commerce Bill](<https://www.nyasatimes.com/minister-chipungu-reveals-hackers-targeted-malawis-land-database/>). The text of the Act names no regulation made under it, and none made has been found beyond drafts. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Namibia's [Electronic Transactions Act 4 of 2019 was published in the Government Gazette on 29 November 2019](<http://www.lac.org.na/laws/2019/7068.pdf>). [Most of it came into force on 16 March 2020](<http://www.lac.org.na/laws/2019/7068.pdf>). In the last twelve months, the minister [made the Electronic Signature Regulations under section 20 on 27 November 2025](<https://www.lac.org.na/laws/2025/8814.pdf>). On 17 December 2025 CRAN [published regulations on accrediting security products and certification service providers](<https://www.lac.org.na/laws/2025/8808.pdf>). [Section 20 and Chapter 5 came into force on 15 June 2026](<http://www.lac.org.na/laws/2019/7068.pdf>), and DigiNam, the national public key infrastructure, [was launched under the Act on 31 August 2026](<https://economist.com.na/government-launches-diginam-to-revolutionise-digital-security-and-streamline-public-services/>). In September 2026 [CRAN accredited the Ministry of Home Affairs as Namibia's first certification service provider](<https://neweralive.na/home-affairs-becomes-namibias-first-certification-service-provider/>), for four years. No date for Chapter 4 on consumer protection has been found.

Niger's [Loi 2019-03 of 30 April 2019 on electronic transactions](<https://mcnti.gouv.ne/ova_doc/loi-2019-03-du-30-avril-2019-portant-sur-les-transactions-electroniques-au-niger/>) covers electronic signatures, contracts and payments, data retention and sanctions. At a workshop in March 2025 [the minister named an implementing decree, no. 2024-715 of 15 November 2024](<https://www.lesahel.org/atelier-de-renforcement-des-capacites-sur-les-transactions-electroniques-mieux-comprendre-les-textes-regissant-le-e-commerce-le-contrat-par-voie-electronique-au-niger/>), made under the law. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No accreditation of a signature provider, registration of online sellers or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found, and no date of entry into force has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

Nigeria's Cybercrimes Act gives electronic signatures legal effect, and [PLAC Legist says section 17 of the Act, as amended in 2024, sets which transactions are valid by electronic signature](<https://placng.org/Legist/cybercrimes-amendment-act-exposes-lapses-in-legislative-process/>). In the last twelve months, [TechCabal reports](<https://techcabal.com/2026/08/13/nigerias-identity-law-raises-questions-over-digital-signatures/>) that the National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill would give qualifying electronic signatures the same validity as handwritten ones. By May 2026 the House of Representatives had approved it. [In July 2026 the Senate ICT committee chair said the bill was at third reading](<https://www.thisdaylive.com/2026/07/09/national-digital-economy-and-e-governance-act-2026-ready-in-weeks/>), with assent expected within weeks. No source found names rules made under the Cybercrimes Act on electronic signatures. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Rwanda's [Law 011/2026 of 26 February 2026 on competition and consumer protection](<https://www.rica.gov.rw/fileadmin/user_upload/RICA/Publications/Laws/OG_n___Special_of_04.03.2026__Ihiganwa_mu_bucuruzi_no_kurengera_umuguzi__1___1___1_.pdf>) carries a chapter on e-commerce, from Article 41 onward, setting obligations for an e-commerce enterprise and for an online intermediary. It came into force on its publication in the Official Gazette on 4 March 2026. In the last twelve months, the e-commerce chapter has applied from that date. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Sudan's Electronic Transactions Act of 2007, with its amendments, is the law cited in the [SudaPass terms of use](<https://sudapass.gov.sd/terms?lang=en>), published on 21 May 2026. They state that a digital signature meeting its requirements is equivalent to a handwritten signature (Article 8), and they cite its Article 28 for punishing forgery. In the last twelve months, these terms are the one use of the Act found in a government service. No decree, regulation or order made under the Act has been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Senegal's [Law no. 2008-08 of 25 January 2008 on electronic transactions](<https://www.vie-publique.sn/docs/e39e7d8a-b4c7-41f7-b3e5-eb3429a364d6/loi-n-2008-08-du-25-janvier-2008-sur-les-transactions-electroniques-au-senegal.pdf>) gives electronic records and signatures equivalence with paper. It also sets rules for electronic commerce. [Decree no. 2008-718 of 30 June 2008 on electronic commerce](<https://www.osiris.sn/Decret-no-2008-718-du-30-juin-2008.html>) was made to apply it. In the last twelve months the law was cited and not changed: in March 2026 [the justice minister named it in Senegal's legal framework](<https://senego.com/digitalisation-de-la-justice-des-services-desormais-accessibles-en-ligne-pour-les-citoyens_1941148.html>), as the law that recognises digital documents. No accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

Sierra Leone's Electronic Transactions Act, Act 89 of 2019, is in force, and the [SierraLII record](<https://old.sierralii.org/sl/legislation/act/2019/89-0>) gives assent and commencement on 5 December 2019. [Sierra Loaded reports](<https://sierraloaded.sl/news/government-activate-e-transactions-law/>) that the Act gives legal recognition to electronic signatures, consumer protection and digital communications in courts. In the last twelve months, at a government dialogue on 27 and 28 July 2026 on implementing the Act, its enforcement structures were not yet fully established. These include digital certification authorities, electronic evidence procedures, dispute resolution and penalties. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

In August 2026 a Ministry of Information adviser wrote, in an article [published on 19 August 2026](<https://sonna.so/en/article/Somalia%E2%80%99s-Most-Valuable-Chinese-Tech-Import-Is-Not-a-Model-It-Is-a-Megawatt>) and in a personal capacity, that Somalia's E-Transactions Law is moving through the legislative process. In the last twelve months, [in October 2026 the communications ministry said the House of the People had approved the Digital Transactions Bill by 137 votes](<https://www.africa-newsroom.com/press/somalias-house-of-the-people-approves-the-digital-transactions-bill-with-137-votes-in-favour>). The Senate stage and assent are not stated. No law in force on electronic transactions or e-commerce has been found. Establishing would need a law in force on electronic contracts, signatures or online sales.

In April 2025 the World Bank said that [an E-Signature Law has been passed](<https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099041125035024996/pdf/P177158-11847402-82b3-4460-9bf4-0fe106ed4291.pdf>) in São Tomé and Príncipe. [A World Bank mission note of September 2025 describes an electronic signature service, Assinatura Electrónica](<https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099102025185177863/pdf/P177158-d0ebd79d-6646-4e92-b9ae-1183b632c15a.pdf>). It was built by INIC and the registry office DGRN. In the last twelve months, on 27 October 2026 the justice minister listed [an e-commerce bill](<https://rafa.tl/pt/sao-tome-e-principe-defende-mecanismos-mais-rapidos-para-obter-provas-digitais-entre-paises-da-cplp/>) in preparation, financed by the World Bank. No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

[The Prime Minister said in October 2025 that the Electronic Transactions Act was passed in 2022](<https://eswatinipositivenews.online/cybersecurity-key-to-national-security-and-growth-pm/>). [APC, in an article published on 22 July 2024](<https://www.apc.org/en/news/risk-human-rights-infringement-eswatini-rushes-regulate-ict-sector>), lists the Electronic Communications Transactions Act of 2022 among the ICT laws the regulator ESCCOM oversees. In the last twelve months the Act was cited and not changed: on 29 April 2026 [Minister Savannah Maziya listed the Electronic Transactions Act of 2022 among Eswatini's existing legal groundwork](<https://swazi24.com/44934/news/maziya-opens-push-for-national-data-policy/>). No decree, regulation or order made under the law has been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Seychelles' [Electronic Transactions Act, 2001 (Act 8 of 2001)](<https://seylii.org/akn/sc/act/2001/8/eng@2018-03-29/source>) commenced on 20 December 2001. It gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures. In May 2025 [the Supreme Court held that the Act provides the legal framework for digital signatures](<https://www.judiciary.sc/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/23052025-cc19_2025-ralph-lablache-vs-antine-lablache.pdf>). The consolidated text, current to 29 March 2018, lists Statutory Instrument 12 of 2024 as an outstanding amendment. No change has been found in the last twelve months. The text names no regulation on electronic signatures, on those who certify them or on those who sell online. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Chad's Law No. 008/PR/2015 on electronic transactions is listed in [the regulator ARCEP's register of laws](<https://arcep.td/lois.html>), which gives its year, 2015. In the last twelve months, [Article 53 of Law No. 008/AN/SENAT/2025, the finance law for 2026](<https://ecofinances.gouv.td/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Loi-n008-AN-SENAT-2025-Portant-loi-de-Finances-2026-LF-2026.pdf>), made electronic signature compulsory for administrative correspondence in the finance ministry from 1 January 2026. It states that this signature has the same legal value as a handwritten one. No decree, regulation or order made under the 2015 law has been found. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Togo's [Decree 2018-062/PR of 21 March 2018](<https://arcep.tg/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Decret_2018_062_PR_portant_reglementation_des_transactions_services_electronique.pdf>) was made in application of Law 2017-007 of 22 June 2017 on electronic transactions. It has 105 articles and covers formalities for e-commerce sellers in Article 6, electronic signatures and qualified certificates, trust service providers and the accreditation procedure. [Law 2023-012 of 19 July 2023](<https://arcep.tg/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Loi-n2023_012-du-19-juillet-2023-de-2023-portant-modification-de-la-loi-sur-les-transactions-electroniques.pdf>) amends the 2017 law. No change has been found in the last twelve months. No accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

Tunisia's [Law no. 2000-83 of 9 August 2000 on electronic exchanges and commerce](<https://www.cmf.tn/sites/default/files/pdfs/reglementation/textes-reference/loi_2000-83_090800_fr.pdf>) gives electronic documents and signatures legal effect and creates the national electronic certification agency ANCE. [Decree-law 2020-31 of 10 June 2020](<https://www.marchespublics.gov.tn/fr/legislations/5923/download>) gives a reliable electronic signature the same evidentiary force as a handwritten one. The ID4Africa country playbook of May 2026 reports that [decrees of 2000-2001 organise certification and the accreditation of certification providers](<https://id4africa.com/2026/files/T1-3-2-Tunisia-FINAL.pdf>). No change has been found in the last twelve months. No accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law in the last three years has been dated. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

The communications ministry says [the government enacted the Act in 2015](<https://www.mawasiliano.go.tz/pages/completed-project>). That is Tanzania's Electronic Transactions Act, Chapter 442. In the last twelve months, [Part III of the Finance Act, 2026, published on 30 June 2026, amends section 13 of the Act](<https://oagmis.oag.go.tz/portal/acts/337/download>) and leaves the rest standing. It is an act of parliament, not a regulation or order made under the Act. Its text names no regulation on electronic signatures, on those who certify them or on those who sell online. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

Uganda's [Electronic Transactions Act](<https://ulii.org/akn/ug/act/2011/8/eng@2011-03-18>) (Act 8 of 2011, now Chapter 99) commenced on 15 April 2011. It gives data messages, electronic signatures and electronic contracts legal effect and sets consumer rules for online sellers. The Minister responsible for ICT made the [Electronic Transactions Regulations, 2013 (S.I. 2013 No. 42)](<https://ict.go.ug/public/site/documents/Electronic-Transction-Regulations-SI-42-of-2013.pdf>) on 10 September 2013 under section 35 of the Act. In the last twelve months the Act was cited and not changed: in October 2026 the [Daily Monitor said Uganda relies on a piecemeal framework including the Act](<https://www.monitor.co.ug/uganda/news/national/uganda-champions-au-single-digital-market-plan-to-boost-cross-border-trade-5634362>). No accreditation, licence or penalty under the law in the last three years has been found. Mature would need an accreditation, licence, registration or penalty under the law.

South Africa's law is the Electronic Communications and Transactions Act of 2002. [Home Affairs listed it in May 2025](<https://www.id4africa.com/2025/files/PS5A-S1-1-SouthAfrica_FINAL.pdf>) as the law that regulates electronic transactions, and no bill to replace it is named. [TechCentral reported on 11 September 2026](<https://techcentral.co.za/south-africa-behind-neighbours-digital-id/286057/>) that the South African Accreditation Authority accredits providers of advanced electronic signatures under it. Altron Security, TrustFactory and Impression Signatures hold accreditation, and the report gives no date for any of them. No change has been found in the last twelve months. Operating would need a regulation made under the Act.

Zambia's law is the [Electronic Communications and Transactions Act No. 4 of 2021](<https://efficacynews.africa/2026/09/30/govt-reviews-electronic-communications-and-transactions-act/>), which gives a legal framework for electronic transactions and secure electronic signatures. Cabinet approved amendments to it in principle in September 2025. In the last twelve months, as reported on 30 September 2026, the Ministry of Technology and Science began consulting stakeholders on them. The regulator ZICTA [was designated National Root Certification Authority under the Act](<https://efficacynews.africa/2026/09/30/govt-reviews-electronic-communications-and-transactions-act/>), and on 7 September 2026 [the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Technology and Science said the Act provided its legal foundation](<https://zambia24.com/2026/09/07/zambia-bets-on-digital-trust/>) for the national public key infrastructure. No regulation made under the Act is named. Operating would need a decree, regulation or order made under the law.

[FinMark Trust said on 18 June 2026](<https://finmark.org.za/knowledge-hub/blog/building-a-cross-border-dpi-for-financial-inclusion-in-sadc>) that Zimbabwe does not have comprehensive legislation of the kind an Electronic Transactions Act provides. A [first draft of the Electronic Transactions and Electronic Commerce Bill, dated 11 June 2013, is an ITU-assisted government draft](<http://www.techzim.co.zw/wp-content/uploads/2016/08/ZImbabwes-draft-Electronic-Transactions-Electronic-Commerce-Bill.pdf>). It covers legal recognition of electronic communications and signatures, electronic contracts, online consumer protection and service provider liability. The President's address of October 2025 named the bill. In the last twelve months, in February 2026 [Veritas reported that it had been neither presented in Parliament nor published in the Gazette](<https://www.veritaszim.net/node/7858>). No law in force has been found. Establishing would need a law in force on electronic contracts, signatures or online sales.
